principles.name: Create the future
principles.description: Builders and inventors driven by deep empathy for customers. Look around the corner, welcome new ideas, and make bold bets real.
evidence_signals: Proposed or built something new from a customer insight, not just a request
Took a bold bet and explains how the risk was managed
Shows curiosity about where the product or technology (for example AI) is going

principles.name: Own the outcome
principles.description: Think and act like an owner. Take initiative, bias toward action, and own the end result, not just your part.
evidence_signals: Took initiative on a problem nobody assigned
Followed through after launch and fixed what broke
Talks about the business result, not only the task completed

principles.name: Raise the bar
principles.description: Aim high and play to win. Focus relentlessly on execution, celebrate excellence, and be intellectually honest about where to improve.
evidence_signals: Raised quality or performance with a measurable before and after
Admits honestly where the work fell short and what changed
Holds self and team to a high standard of execution
Names a real mistake or hard feedback and shows what was learned from it

principles.name: Be genuine
principles.description: Be yourself, embrace and respect diversity, and support and challenge each other by being honest and direct.
evidence_signals: Included or supported people with different views or backgrounds
Speaks in their own voice and is clear about what they did versus the team or tools such as AI
Credits collaborators instead of presenting team work as solely their own

rounds.name: Talent partner screen
rounds.notes: Adobe's official process calls this the talent conversation: background, career goals, the role and what success looks like. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Online assessment
rounds.notes: Sometimes required, mainly for early-career roles. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Hiring manager screen
rounds.notes: Resume projects, technical deep dive on past decisions, ownership and impact, culture fit.

rounds.name: Coding (data structures and algorithms)
rounds.notes: Usually two rounds. Live coding. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Low-level / object-oriented design
rounds.notes: Design and code classes for a system such as an in-memory file system or rental platform. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: System design
rounds.notes: High-level design; senior candidates get problems grounded in Adobe products (document services, large assets, AI features).

rounds.name: Director / leadership round
rounds.notes: Behavioral and leadership questions, sometimes with a high-level design discussion.

rounds.name: Recruiter screen
rounds.notes: Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Hiring manager screen
rounds.notes: Background, past products and motivation.

rounds.name: Product design case
rounds.notes: Design or improve a product for a user segment; MVP scope and success metrics.

rounds.name: Analytics and metrics
rounds.notes: Subscription, trial conversion and engagement metrics; diagnosing metric changes.

rounds.name: Technical collaboration
rounds.notes: How the PM works with engineering and reasons about technical trade-offs.

rounds.name: Talent partner screen
rounds.notes: ML or research background, publications, interest in creative or document AI. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Technical screen (ML fundamentals)
rounds.notes: Verbal ML and statistics fundamentals (overfitting, evaluation, model choice); some teams add a short coding problem.

rounds.name: Research or project deep dive
rounds.notes: Walk through a past research or production ML project: novelty versus existing methods, results, own contribution. Research roles often present this as a talk to the team.

rounds.name: Coding
rounds.notes: Algorithms in Python, around medium difficulty. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: ML system design
rounds.interviewer_role: Senior ML engineer or principal scientist
rounds.notes: Design an ML feature for an Adobe-style product (image editing, generative media, asset search), covering data, training, serving cost and evaluation.

rounds.name: Behavioral and team fit
rounds.notes: Collaboration with product teams, failed experiments, mentoring.

rounds.name: Talent partner screen
rounds.notes: Background, portfolio highlights and goals. Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Hiring manager conversation
rounds.notes: Background, motivation, problem solving and fit; Adobe calls it a two-way conversation.

rounds.name: Portfolio presentation
rounds.interviewer_role: Panel of designers and design managers
rounds.notes: Present one or two case studies: problem and outcome first, own role, collaboration with PM and engineering, trade-offs and lessons. Panel asks probing follow-ups.

rounds.name: Design exercise or creative brief
rounds.notes: Official page lists creative briefs, design thinking exercises or case study presentations. Some teams give a take-home first, then a presentation and critique.

rounds.name: Cross-functional partner interviews
rounds.notes: How the designer works with partners, handles feedback and disagreement, and what motivates them.

rounds.name: Recruiter screen
rounds.notes: Not simulated in v1.

rounds.name: Hiring manager screen
rounds.notes: Two or three complex cross-functional programs: scope, dependencies, risks and outcome.

rounds.name: Program execution scenario
rounds.notes: Plan a multi-team program (for example a platform migration or an AI capability across products), manage slipping dependencies and risks.

rounds.name: Technical depth
rounds.notes: High-level system design and technical trade-offs; depth varies by team, and some candidates report no technical round.

rounds.name: Stakeholder and leadership
rounds.notes: Cross-team conflict, communicating risk and bad news to leaders, holding owners accountable.

question_patterns.pattern: A time the candidate improved a process or solved a problem on their own initiative
A disagreement within the team and how the candidate handled it honestly and respectfully
A time the candidate pushed work to a higher standard than required and measured the difference
How the candidate would handle a strong performer who is hurting team health or engagement
Walk through a project on the resume: architecture, obstacles, own decisions and measurable impact
How the candidate would deliver a project with far fewer people or time than estimated
Why Adobe, and how the candidate would contribute to the company's next big bets
Design a service for rich documents or large binary assets with versioning, sync and collaboration
Design a common backend component such as a cache, queue or search suggestion service and discuss scaling
Design how a generative AI feature is served to many users while balancing latency and compute cost
Adapt an existing creative or document product for a specific user segment or market
Define how to measure success for a product or feature, including subscription and engagement metrics
The candidate's worst work mistake or hardest feedback, how they responded, and what changed afterwards
What frustrates the candidate at work, how colleagues would notice, and how they work with design, product and engineering partners
Why a showcased project mattered, who it affected, how the candidate learned their needs, and what the candidate personally contributed
What drives the candidate, an area where they have not yet had room to grow, and how this role could help
A concrete example of how the candidate used AI to improve their own work, in their own words
The candidate's most important research or ML contribution, its novelty against existing methods, and how it reached a product
How the candidate runs a multi-team program when dependencies slip or commitments are at risk
Design an ML system for an image, video or asset feature, covering data, model choice, evaluation, and serving latency and cost
Redesign a workflow in a complex professional tool so new users can start easily without slowing down experts

sample_questions.question: Give an example of a time you took the initiative to improve a process or fix a problem at work.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Pick a problem nobody owned. Describe how you noticed it, sized the cost, and acted without waiting. Explain how you got buy-in, what you changed, and the measurable result (time saved, incidents reduced). Show follow-through after the change. Pitfall: an improvement that was really your assigned task.

looking_for: Whether you act on problems nobody owns
How you size the cost of a problem before fixing it
strong_signals: Shows how you got buy-in from others
Ends with a measured result and follow-through
watch_outs: An improvement that was really your assigned work
No numbers on what changed

sample_questions.question: How would you deal with a manager on your team who is very strong technically but has very low team engagement scores?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Start by understanding, not judging: look at the feedback, talk to the manager and the team. Separate technical credibility from people leadership. Give direct, specific feedback, agree on a plan (coaching, delegation, 1:1 practice), and set check-in points with measures. Say what you would do if it does not improve. Show care for both the person and the team.

looking_for: How you coach a manager whose team is disengaged
Whether you seek to understand before you judge
strong_signals: Separates technical skill from people leadership
Sets a clear plan with check-ins and measures
watch_outs: Jumping straight to removing the manager
Ignoring how the team feels

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a disagreement in your team and how you handled it.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Choose a real disagreement with stakes. Show you understood the other view, argued with data, stayed respectful and direct, and helped the team reach a decision. Describe the outcome and the relationship afterwards. Pitfall: a story where you simply won.

looking_for: How you handle real disagreement on a team
Whether you argue with data and stay respectful
strong_signals: Explains the other view fairly
Describes the decision and the relationship afterwards
watch_outs: A story where you simply won
A disagreement with no real stakes

sample_questions.question: The estimate for a project is 9 people for 9 months, but you have 3 people and 3 months. How would you deliver it?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify the real goal and the must-have outcome. Cut scope to an MVP, sequence by risk and value, and reuse existing components or buy where possible. Be explicit about what you drop and the quality bar you keep. Negotiate with stakeholders openly and set checkpoints. Show judgment, not heroics. Pitfall: promising everything by working nights.

looking_for: How you deliver under hard limits on people and time
Whether you cut scope with judgment, not heroics
strong_signals: Defines the must-have outcome and an MVP
Says openly what gets dropped and keeps a quality bar
watch_outs: Promising everything by working nights
Not involving stakeholders in the trade-offs

sample_questions.question: What do you think Adobe's big future bets are, and how would you help with them in this role?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Show real research: for example generative AI in creative and document products, cloud collaboration, and digital experience. Link one bet to the team you would join and to your concrete skills. Offer one thoughtful idea or question. Pitfall: generic praise of the brand.

looking_for: Whether you have researched where the company is heading
How you connect its bets to your own skills
strong_signals: Links one specific bet to the team you would join
Offers a thoughtful idea or question
watch_outs: Generic praise of the brand
Naming bets with no link to your role

sample_questions.question: Describe a past project you are proud of.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Pick a project at the scope of the target level. Explain the problem, your role, two key decisions with trade-offs, and measurable impact for users or the business. Be ready for deep technical follow-ups on the architecture. Say what you would do differently.

looking_for: The depth and scope of your past work
How you make and explain key decisions
strong_signals: Covers two decisions with their trade-offs
Gives measurable impact and what you would change
watch_outs: A project below the level you are applying for
Not being ready for deep technical follow-ups

sample_questions.question: Explain the architecture of your current project and the main obstacles you have faced in your role.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Give a short system overview with the main components and data flow. Pick one or two real obstacles (technical or organizational), what you did, and the outcome. Show you understand why the system is built as it is. Pitfall: blaming others for obstacles.

looking_for: Whether you understand why your system is built as it is
How you deal with real obstacles
strong_signals: Gives a short, clear overview of components and data flow
Describes what you did about an obstacle and the result
watch_outs: Getting lost in detail before the big picture
Blaming others for obstacles

sample_questions.question: Why do you want to join Adobe?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Connect a specific product or technology area to your experience and goals. Mention what you would bring in the first months. Be genuine; Adobe's own interview tips stress real interest in the products and curious questions.

looking_for: Whether your interest in the company is genuine
How your experience fits a specific product area
strong_signals: Names a specific product or technology you care about
Says what you would bring in your first months
watch_outs: An answer that fits any company
Talking only about perks or prestige

sample_questions.question: Design a cloud document service for files with complex internal structure such as layers and embedded assets, supporting version history, sync across devices and collaborative editing.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify document sizes, users per document and offline needs. Model the document as a tree of components so changes are small deltas. Store large assets separately (object storage, content-addressed chunks). Version with an operation log plus periodic snapshots. Sync deltas, and choose a conflict strategy (OT, CRDT, or per-component locking) with reasons. Cover permissions, undo, and storage cost. Pitfall: re-uploading whole files on every change.

looking_for: How you model a complex document for sync and versioning
How you choose a conflict strategy for collaboration
strong_signals: Treats changes as small deltas, not whole files
Keeps large assets apart from document structure
Explains the trade-offs of the conflict approach
watch_outs: Re-uploading the whole file on every change
Skipping permissions, undo or storage cost

sample_questions.question: Design a pipeline to store and deliver very large binary creative assets to users around the world.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Cover chunked, resumable uploads, content hashing and dedup, object storage with lifecycle tiers, metadata store, thumbnail and preview generation jobs, CDN delivery with cache keys and invalidation, and delta sync for edits. Discuss cost versus latency and regional replication. Strong answers quantify sizes and bandwidth.

looking_for: How you move very large files reliably around the world
How you balance cost against latency
strong_signals: Covers resumable chunked uploads and deduplication
Puts numbers on file sizes and bandwidth
Plans CDN caching and invalidation
watch_outs: Treating huge files like small API payloads
No plan for edits or regional copies

sample_questions.question: Design the backend for a generative AI image feature used inside a creative app at large scale.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify latency targets and request volume. Describe a request gateway, queueing, GPU inference pool with autoscaling and batching, result storage and delivery. Cover quotas and entitlement checks, content safety filtering, caching repeated prompts, and graceful degradation. The key trade-off is interactive latency versus GPU cost; state how you balance it and what you would measure.

looking_for: How you serve an expensive model at large scale
How you trade interactive latency against GPU cost
strong_signals: Covers queueing, batching and autoscaling of inference
Includes quotas, safety filtering and graceful degradation
watch_outs: Ignoring cost or capacity limits
No content safety or entitlement checks

sample_questions.question: Design a typeahead search box that suggests completions as the user types.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Requirements: latency budget per keystroke, ranking by popularity, personalization, freshness. Data structure: prefix trie or precomputed top-k per prefix. Serving: in-memory shards, client debouncing, caching common prefixes. Offline pipeline to rebuild counts from logs. Discuss trade-offs of freshness versus cost and how to filter bad suggestions.

looking_for: How you meet a tight latency budget per keystroke
Your choice of data structure for prefix lookups
strong_signals: Explains ranking, freshness and how counts get rebuilt
Uses caching and client debouncing to cut load
watch_outs: Querying a database on every keystroke
No plan to filter bad suggestions

sample_questions.question: Design a message queue for communication between services.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify delivery guarantees (at-least-once, ordering per key), throughput and retention. Describe producers, partitioned append-only logs, consumer groups with offsets, replication and leader election, acknowledgments and retries, dead-letter handling. Discuss back-pressure and the trade-off between durability and latency.

looking_for: Whether you clarify delivery and ordering guarantees first
How you design for durability and throughput
strong_signals: Covers partitions, consumer offsets and replication
Handles retries, dead letters and back-pressure
watch_outs: Vague about at-least-once versus exactly-once
No answer for a node failure

sample_questions.question: Design a caching layer that runs across multiple nodes.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Cover consistent hashing for key placement, replication for hot keys, eviction policy, TTLs, and invalidation on writes (write-through, write-behind or cache-aside) with consistency trade-offs. Discuss node failure and rebalancing, thundering herd protection, and metrics such as hit rate.

looking_for: How you spread keys across nodes
How you keep the cache consistent with the source of truth
strong_signals: Explains consistent hashing and rebalancing
Chooses an invalidation strategy and states its trade-off
Protects against hot keys and thundering herds
watch_outs: Ignoring what happens when a node fails
No metrics such as hit rate

sample_questions.question: Design a warehouse management system where storage spaces are rented to different firms and orders for their stored items must be processed efficiently.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify entities (warehouse, space, firm, item, order) and the key operations. Model data and APIs, then the allocation strategy for spaces (fit, fragmentation) and order processing flow with concurrency control. Discuss scale, consistency for inventory counts, and extensibility. A reported pitfall is weak structure; break the problem into components early.

looking_for: How you break an open-ended system into components
How you model entities and core operations
strong_signals: Defines the data model and APIs early
Handles concurrency on inventory and allocation
watch_outs: Weak structure that jumps between topics
Skipping consistency of stock counts

sample_questions.question: How would you position Creative Cloud to win small businesses in a specific Asian market such as Singapore?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify goal (new subscribers, revenue). Segment small businesses by need (social content, print, web). Size the opportunity roughly. Identify barriers: price, skills, local payment, competition from simpler tools. Propose a focused offer (templates, simpler app, bundles, partners) and a go-to-market. Define metrics: trial starts, conversion, retention. Recommend one path with risks.

looking_for: How you frame a go-to-market problem in a new market
Whether you segment customers by need
strong_signals: Sizes the opportunity roughly and names local barriers
Recommends one focused path with metrics and risks
watch_outs: A generic plan that ignores the local market
No clear goal or success metric

sample_questions.question: How would you measure the success of a short-video feature in a social app?
sample_questions.strong_answer: State the feature goal first. Pick a north star (for example time spent watching or creators posting weekly) and supporting metrics for creators, viewers and the business. Add guardrails such as impact on other surfaces. Explain how to attribute change (experiments, cohorts). Pitfall: a long list of metrics with no hierarchy.

looking_for: Whether you start from the feature's goal
How you build a hierarchy of metrics
strong_signals: Picks a clear north star with supporting metrics
Adds guardrails and a way to attribute change
watch_outs: A long list of metrics with no priority
Ignoring creators or the wider app

sample_questions.question: What is the worst mistake you have made at work, or the hardest feedback you have received, and how did you respond?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Pick a real mistake with consequences, not a disguised strength. Own your part plainly, without blaming others. Explain how you reacted in the moment, what you did to repair the damage, and the concrete habit or process you changed afterwards. Give credit to anyone who helped. Close with evidence the change stuck. Pitfall: saying you cannot think of a failure.

looking_for: Self-awareness and humility about your own mistakes
How you respond to hard feedback
strong_signals: Owns their part without blaming others
Names the habit or process that changed afterwards
watch_outs: A disguised strength instead of a real mistake
Being unable to name any failure

sample_questions.question: What makes you frustrated at work, and how would your teammates be able to tell?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Answer honestly with a real trigger (for example unclear decisions or late changes). Show you know how it shows up in your behavior, how you manage it, and how you tell partners what you need. Link it to how you work with design, product and engineering. Pitfall: a polished non-answer that reveals nothing about you.

looking_for: Self-awareness about your work style
How you manage frustration with partners
strong_signals: Names a real trigger and how it shows
Explains how you communicate what you need
watch_outs: A polished answer that reveals nothing
Blaming colleagues for your reactions

sample_questions.question: Walk me through one project from your portfolio: why did it matter, who did it affect, and how did you come to understand their needs?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Open with the problem and the outcome, then the people affected and how you learned about them (research, data, support tickets). Make your own role clear versus the team's. Show two key decisions with the options you rejected, how you worked with PM and engineering, and the measured result. End with what you learned and would change. Pitfall: a tour of polished screens with no problem context.

looking_for: Whether the work solved a real problem for real people
What you personally contributed
strong_signals: Starts with the problem and the outcome
Shows decisions, trade-offs and collaboration with partners
watch_outs: Polished screens with no problem context
Vague about own role versus the team

sample_questions.question: Is there an area where you have not yet had the chance to grow, and how could this role help you with it?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Name a specific, honest gap that matters for your career, why you have not developed it yet, and what you are already doing about it. Connect it to something real about the role or team. Show you would also bring strengths in return. Pitfall: naming a gap that is central to the job without a plan.

looking_for: Honesty about your own development
Whether the role fits your growth
strong_signals: Names a specific gap and steps already taken
Links it to something real about the team
watch_outs: A fake weakness
A gap that is core to the job with no plan

sample_questions.question: From where you stand, what would you improve about Adobe or its products, and why do you want to work here?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Show research on one product or strategy area. Offer one specific, respectful improvement grounded in user evidence or your own use, with the trade-off it carries. Connect your motivation to the team's work and what you would bring. Pitfall: harsh criticism with no reasoning, or flattery with no idea.

looking_for: Whether you have researched the company and team
Whether you can critique thoughtfully
strong_signals: One specific improvement grounded in evidence
Motivation tied to the team's actual work
watch_outs: Flattery with no idea
Criticism with no reasoning

sample_questions.question: Give a concrete example of how you have used AI to improve your own work.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Describe one real task, the tool and how you used it, and the measurable effect (time saved, quality, new options). Explain where you checked or overrode its output and what stayed your own judgment. Mention a limit or risk you noticed. Pitfall: listing AI tools with no example, or an answer that sounds written by a tool.

looking_for: Real, applied use of AI rather than a list of tools
Your own judgment on top of the tool
strong_signals: One concrete task with a measured effect
Says where the output was checked or overridden
watch_outs: Listing tools with no example
No awareness of limits or risks

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a time user research contradicted what your stakeholders believed. What did you do?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Set up the belief and why stakeholders held it. Explain the research method and why the finding was credible. Show how you shared it: early, with evidence, and respecting their goals. Describe the decision reached, any compromise, and the result. Pitfall: treating stakeholders as opponents.

looking_for: How you use evidence to change minds
How you keep stakeholder trust
strong_signals: Explains why the finding was credible
Describes the decision and the result
watch_outs: Treating stakeholders as opponents
No outcome

sample_questions.question: How would you redesign the main toolbar of a professional image editor so new users can get started without slowing down expert users?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify the user segments and the goal (activation of new users without hurting pro retention). Use evidence of where newcomers get stuck. Consider progressive disclosure, contextual tools, search for commands, and customizable workspaces. Protect expert speed (shortcuts, muscle memory). Define success metrics for both groups and plan testing with real users. Recommend one direction with trade-offs.

looking_for: How you design for two very different user groups
Whether you ground ideas in user evidence
strong_signals: Protects expert speed while easing onboarding
Defines metrics for both groups and a test plan
watch_outs: Simplifying by removing power features
Jumping to visuals before framing the problem

sample_questions.question: Design AI suggestions inside a creative app that help users without interrupting their creative flow.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Define the user and the moments where help is wanted. Choose when to suggest (on request, at natural pauses) and how (non-modal, easy to dismiss, previewable, undoable). Address trust: explain the suggestion, keep user control, handle low-quality results. Define metrics such as acceptance rate, undo rate and task completion, with a guardrail on interruptions. Pitfall: pop-ups that break concentration.

looking_for: How you balance help against interruption
How you keep the user in control of AI output
strong_signals: Chooses timing and form of suggestions deliberately
Measures acceptance and undo, with guardrails
watch_outs: Modal pop-ups that break concentration
No plan for poor suggestions

sample_questions.question: Design an ML system that removes the background from photos with high accuracy.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify inputs (resolution, hair and fine edges, video or still) and latency targets (interactive or batch). Frame it as segmentation or matting; discuss labeled data, synthetic compositing for training, and model choice. Cover evaluation (IoU, edge quality, human review), on-device versus cloud serving, and a fallback for user correction. Discuss the accuracy versus latency and cost trade-off.

looking_for: How you frame the ML problem and the data
How you evaluate quality on hard edges
strong_signals: Plans training data and evaluation metrics
Weighs on-device against cloud serving
watch_outs: Naming a model with no data or evaluation plan
Ignoring latency for interactive use

sample_questions.question: How would you build semantic search over a large library of creative assets such as images, videos and templates?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify query types (text, image), library size and freshness. Use multimodal embeddings, an offline pipeline to embed new assets, and an approximate nearest neighbor index. Combine with metadata filters and keyword search, then rerank. Cover evaluation (relevance judgments, click data), permissions, and cost of embedding and storage. Discuss index updates and latency.

looking_for: How you represent and index mixed media
How you measure search relevance
strong_signals: Uses embeddings plus filters and reranking
Plans relevance evaluation and index updates
watch_outs: Skipping permissions on private assets
No way to measure relevance

sample_questions.question: How have you balanced model accuracy against inference latency in a production ML system?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Describe a real system with its latency budget and quality metric. Explain the options you tried (smaller model, distillation, quantization, caching, batching, cascades) and the measured effect of each. Show how you chose the operating point with product partners and monitored it after launch. Pitfall: optimizing one metric with no business context.

looking_for: How you trade quality against speed and cost
Whether you measured each option
strong_signals: States the latency budget and quality metric
Explains the chosen operating point and monitoring
watch_outs: Only one metric with no business context
No numbers

sample_questions.question: How would you evaluate the quality of AI-generated images or other creative content?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Separate dimensions: fidelity to the prompt, visual quality, diversity, safety and brand or legal constraints. Combine automatic metrics (prompt-alignment scores, distribution metrics) with structured human ratings and side-by-side comparisons. Explain sampling, rater agreement, and how offline scores link to user signals such as downloads or regenerations. Note the limits of each metric.

looking_for: How you define quality for generated media
How you combine metrics with human judgment
strong_signals: Splits quality into clear dimensions
Links offline scores to user behavior
watch_outs: Relying on one automatic metric
Ignoring safety and rights

sample_questions.question: What is your most important research contribution, what is new about it compared with existing methods, and why does it matter?
sample_questions.strong_answer: State the problem and the prior state of the art in two sentences. Explain the core idea, the evidence (benchmarks, ablations), and your own part versus co-authors. Be honest about limits. Then explain the impact: adoption, follow-up work, or a path into a product. Pitfall: listing papers without explaining the idea.

looking_for: Whether you can explain the novelty clearly
Your own contribution versus co-authors
strong_signals: Compares cleanly with prior methods
Admits limits and shows impact
watch_outs: Listing papers without the core idea
Overclaiming results

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a research or ML project that did not work out. What did you learn?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Pick a real dead end. Explain the hypothesis, the signals that it was failing, and when and how you decided to stop or pivot. Share what you salvaged (data, tools, negative results) and how it changed how you choose or de-risk projects. Pitfall: blaming data or compute without reflection.

looking_for: How you recognize and handle a failing project
What you learned from it
strong_signals: Explains the decision to stop or pivot
Shows what changed in later projects
watch_outs: Blaming data or compute
A project that actually succeeded

sample_questions.question: How would you lead a program to bring a generative AI capability into several products at the same time?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify the goal, launch date and which products are in scope. Set up a shared platform team and per-product owners, a dependency map, and milestones. Address model capacity, safety and legal review, and consistent user experience. Define a risk register, a decision process, and launch metrics. Explain how you sequence products (pilot first) and report status to leaders.

looking_for: How you structure a large multi-team program
How you manage shared dependencies
strong_signals: Pilots first, then sequences other products
Covers capacity, safety review and launch metrics
watch_outs: A plan with no owners or decision process
Ignoring legal and safety review

sample_questions.question: A program you run has key dependencies on other teams that are at risk of slipping. How do you handle it?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Confirm the facts and the impact on the critical path. Talk to the owning teams to understand causes. Lay out options (re-sequence, cut scope, add help, change the date) with trade-offs, and escalate early with a recommendation. Agree new commitments and checkpoints, and communicate clearly to stakeholders. Pitfall: hoping it recovers or escalating with no options.

looking_for: How early you spot and act on risk
Whether you bring options, not only problems
strong_signals: Quantifies impact on the critical path
Escalates early with a recommendation
watch_outs: Waiting and hoping
Blaming the other team

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a time you had to tell senior leaders bad news about a program.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Explain the situation and why the news mattered. Show you raised it early and directly, with facts, impact, root cause and a recovery plan with options. Describe how leaders reacted, the decision made and the outcome. Reflect on what you would do to catch it sooner. Pitfall: softening the message until it is unclear.

looking_for: Whether you deliver bad news early and directly
Whether you bring a recovery plan
strong_signals: States facts, impact and options clearly
Reflects on how to catch it sooner
watch_outs: Softening the message until it is unclear
Hiding the problem until it is too late

bar_by_level.scope_expectation: 0 to 1 years (internships, research or projects). Improves quality, performance and reliability of a component with guidance from the team; works independently on well-scoped tasks.
Member of Technical Staff 1 (title used mainly in India). Delivers well-defined tasks with guidance.
Member of Technical Staff 2. Owns features independently inside one team.
4 to 9 years. Designs and builds features end to end in a cloud service, aligns with leadership on priorities, and mentors others on the team.
Around 6 to 8 years for Computer Scientist 2. Owns components or services end to end including production operations and on-call, leads designs, reviews code and mentors junior engineers.
US title. Owns design and implementation of key components of a large-scale platform, joins architecture reviews and drives cross-team efforts. Required experience varies widely by posting.

Technical lead or architect for a product area (one architect posting asks for 14+ years). Leads technical design, vision and implementation strategy, shapes architecture with product and UX, and mentors the team.
12+ years. Sets architectural standards that other teams across Adobe adopt, designs for a multi-year horizon, and influences direction across business units without formal authority.
10+ years. Sets technical direction for a large product or platform, owns end-to-end outcomes such as cost and throughput at very large scale, and influences the organization.
3+ years building and deploying ML solutions. Builds, trains and ships models for a product feature within one team.
Architects end-to-end ML systems, owns the ML lifecycle from features to retraining, and guides technical direction across teams through design reviews and mentoring.
Level IV asks for a PhD plus 3 years or 6 years of experience. Leads research initiatives independently, takes research risks on hard problems, and leads ambitious projects.
Recognized technical leader with 5+ years developing, evaluating and deploying ML models. Leads architecture and technology choices for applied research that ships in products.
Drives defined initiatives in one area (for example pricing and packaging), builds the ROI case and gains cross-functional and executive approval.
Owns a product area, its roadmap and metrics, and leads cross-functional teams.
8+ years. Leads vision, strategy and execution for a large product area through the full lifecycle, and drives strategy across multiple teams and organizations.
7+ years shipping complex products. Owns experience flows for a product area with minimal guidance and leads design decisions with PM and engineering, working from customer requirements.
8+ years including team leadership. Sets direction for a design area, grows designers through coaching, owns delivery quality, and ties design work to measurable business and customer impact.

persona.tone: Warm, professional and two-way; curious about the person as well as the work, and wants to hear the candidate's own voice
persona.pace: Moderate; moves quickly through the resume, then goes deep on one project or portfolio piece with probing follow-ups
persona.pushback_style: Asks for measurable impact and for what the candidate personally did versus the team; probes mistakes, hard feedback and trade-offs; poses 'what would you do?' scenarios and may change requirements mid-design
persona.closing_style: Leaves real time for the candidate's questions about the team, strategy and culture, and notices when a candidate has none

case_style.notes: PM cases center on improving Adobe products for a segment (SMB, new markets) and on subscription, monetization and engagement metrics. Design cases are creative briefs or redesigns of complex pro workflows, presented and critiqued. Estimation is light.

low_confidence_notes: values_framework: Adobe has no dedicated values round; values are probed inside hiring manager and leadership rounds. Adobe's 'AI and your hiring experience' page ties authenticity to 'Be genuine', so the current values are used in hiring, but older careers pages still mention the earlier set (genuine, exceptional, innovative, involved). Principle weights are our estimate.

loop_structure: Adobe's official page confirms the stages (talent conversation, hiring manager, skills assessments and team interviews, with coding, system design, portfolio reviews or creative briefs by role) but not round counts or durations. Round detail comes from candidate reports and prep sites and varies by team and country. The data_ml, design and tpm loops come mainly from CleverPrep; the tpm loop has no official source and some candidates report no technical round.

bar_by_level: Adobe does not publish a ladder. Scope text now comes from current official postings on adobe.wd5.myworkdayjobs.com, which state years of experience and scope by title, but years vary widely between postings (one US Senior Software Engineer posting asks for 15+ years). MTS 1, MTS 2 and the title-to-level mapping still come from third parties. Postings expire, so the cited links may stop working. No TPM postings were open on 2026-10-28, so tpm has no bar entries.

persona: based on Adobe's official Interviewing at Adobe and AI hiring pages and an Adobe Design article in which design managers describe what they ask and look for; that article covers design hiring only, so engineering interviewer style is inferred from candidate reports.

scoring_weights: derived from officially published signals (measurable impact and problem solving on the Interviewing at Adobe page; collaboration, credit sharing, self-awareness and learning from mistakes in the Adobe Design article; own voice on the AI hiring page) mapped to our competencies. No public source gives weights; the numbers are our estimate.

case_style: left low. Adobe confirms that design roles get creative briefs or design exercises and that other roles get scenario-based discussions, but PM case prompts and the product_sense, estimation and system_thinking split come only from third-party guides (one PM example uses a non-Adobe product).

sample_questions: Glassdoor (HTTP 403) and Interview Query (HTTP 429) blocked the fetcher, so ML, research and TPM questions cite CleverPrep, a prep site that aggregates candidate reports. Five questions come from the official Adobe Design article, which reports questions design managers ask; four are tagged for all roles but were reported for design hiring.
